readings.title: Michael Robartes and the Dancer
readings.challenge: Follow a dialogue in which one speaker has most of the words, and weigh the other’s short replies.
readings.focus: An argument that a beautiful woman should think with her body rather than from books.
readings.context: He interprets a painting of a knight killing a dragon to rescue a lady, then argues with She about learning. Athena is the Greek goddess of wisdom; Paul Veronese was a Venetian painter; Michelangelo carved the figures “Morning” and “Night.” Composite means made of parts; blessed souls, in the old theology He cites, are simple.
readings.contentNote: He argues that a beautiful woman should not seek book learning. The view belongs to a character the poem lets the woman answer, and it is open to criticism.

excerpt.locator: Michael Robartes and the Dancer, the title poem, a dialogue of He and She; complete individual work; opens “He”; closes “They say such different things at school.”.

questions.prompt: How does He reinterpret the altar-piece, and what would make the lady “grow wise”?
facilitatorNotes: He says the dragon is the lady’s own thought, which the knight fights every morning. If she turned her eyes to the looking-glass, she would grow wise at once: her wisdom, in his account, lies in her own beauty, not in argument.
evidence: The half-dead dragon was her thought,
She would have time to turn her eyes, Her lover thought, upon the glass And on the instant would grow wise.

questions.prompt: What reasons does He give against her going to college, and what is his evidence?
facilitatorNotes: Books cannot give knowledge with a gravity that fits “that beating breast, / That vigorous thigh.” He points to painters and sculptors whose bodies prove that “all must come to sight and touch.” The evidence is artistic images, which supports a view of beauty but not a conclusion about what women may learn.
evidence: For what mere book can grant a knowledge With an impassioned gravity
That all must come to sight and touch;

questions.prompt: What do her last words, “They say such different things at school,” suggest about who has won?
facilitatorNotes: She may be wryly unconvinced, politely ending the debate, or confused by his scholastic “principles.” Since He began by calling opinion worthless and ends by arguing from a Latin text, her line exposes the irony of his own reasoning. Several readings are defensible; each should account for her shortness.
evidence: Opinion is not worth a rush;
I have principles to prove me right. It follows from this Latin text
They say such different things at school.

readings.title: Solomon and the Witch
readings.challenge: Follow Solomon’s interpretation of a strange cry and decide what the ending does to it.
readings.focus: Love as a struggle to make the imagined and the real coincide.
readings.context: In legend the Queen of Sheba visited King Solomon, famed for wisdom and for understanding the speech of birds. Here “that Arab lady” tells Solomon she cried out in an unknown tongue during the night; the apple is the fruit of the Fall in Genesis.
readings.contentNote: Frank but not explicit treatment of sexual love.

excerpt.locator: Solomon and the Witch; complete individual work; opens “And thus declared that Arab lady: “Last night, where under the wild moon On grassy…”; closes “…where we have lain; And the moon is wilder every minute. Oh, Solomon! let us try again.””.

questions.prompt: What does Solomon say the cockerel’s crow means?
facilitatorNotes: The cockerel crowed before the Fall and would crow again only if Chance and Choice became one and the fallen world ended. Her cry, he suggests, was that crow: their love seemed for a moment to end the world’s division.
evidence: A crested cockerel crew Upon a blossoming apple bough Three hundred years before the Fall,
Chance being at one with Choice at last.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Solomon, is love so often painful?
facilitatorNotes: Each lover brings an imagined image and finds a real one. Lovers test each other with cruelties of Choice and Chance, and even the bride-bed may bring despair. The world ends only when the two images are “a single light.”
evidence: For each an imagined image brings And finds a real image there;
Though several, are a single light, When oil and wick are burned in one;

questions.prompt: “Yet the world stays.” How does the poem’s ending respond to this failure?
facilitatorNotes: Solomon admits the cockerel was wrong, and wonders whether the image was too strong or not strong enough. Sheba answers by describing the night and inviting him to “try again.” The metaphysical failure becomes comic and erotic hope; readers may find the turn playful, moving or both.
evidence: Your cockerel found us in the wrong Although he thought it worth a crow.
Oh, Solomon! let us try again.

readings.title: An Image from a Past Life
readings.challenge: Track what each speaker sees, or claims to see, in the same river at night.
readings.focus: Jealousy, memory and a fear that cannot be reasoned away.
readings.context: A couple stand by a dark river under starlight. In his notes to the book, also in the library, Yeats says he let the woman, not the man, see the figure, because in moments of excitement images pass from one mind to another.

excerpt.locator: An Image from a Past Life, a dialogue of He and She; complete individual work; opens “He”; closes “…the wind, I do not know, that know I am afraid Of the hovering thing night brought me.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening stanza prepare for an “image of poignant recollection”?
facilitatorNotes: Starlight reflected on eddies and a sudden scream from an unseen beast or bird stir him for the first time. The scene mixes beauty with fright, so the image arrives as both memory and alarm.
evidence: The elaborate star-light has thrown reflections On the dark stream,
From terrified, invisible beast or bird:

questions.prompt: What does She see in the water, and why does she cover his eyes?
facilitatorNotes: A “sweetheart from another life” floating among the starry eddies, combing out her hair. She hides it from him because she fears the image of a former love will draw him from her.
evidence: Why have you laid your hands upon my eyes?
A sweetheart from another life floats there

questions.prompt: Does His reassurance answer Her fear? Use the final stanza.
facilitatorNotes: He says any image could only make him fonder of her. She continues to describe the figure throwing up her arms, unsure whether it mocks her, and ends knowing only that she is afraid. Reason does not settle a fear that comes from the night itself; some readers see jealousy, others a genuine apparition, and Yeats’s note suggests she sees an image from his mind.
evidence: But images to make me fonder.
I do not know, that know I am afraid Of the hovering thing night brought me.
